items.title: Porter's framework asks about industry structure, not firms
items.claim: Michael Porter's 1979 HBR article introduced the five forces framework. What does it analyse?

options.text: The structural attractiveness of an industry: rivalry, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes

items.reveal:
Porter's 'How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy' (HBR, March 1979) made a structural argument: average industry profitability is set by the strength of the five forces. Some industries (pharma, software platforms) are persistently profitable; others (airlines, supermarkets) persistently low-margin.

McGahan and Porter (1997) found industry effects explained 19% of business unit profitability variance — less than firm effects (32%) but real. Critics (including Henry Mintzberg) argue the framework underweights innovation, complementors and network effects, which 1979 industry economics didn't see clearly.
items.why: Strategy starts with which industry you're competing in, not how cleverly you compete. Some industries make it nearly impossible to earn supernormal returns.

items.title: PESTLE is a checklist, not a model
items.claim: PESTLE analysis covers Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal and Environmental factors. What is its main analytical limitation?

options.text: It can predict the future with high accuracy
It generates an inventory of factors but does not weight them, link them or model their interactions — students often produce long unprioritised lists
It is legally required for UK firms
It only applies to large firms

items.reveal_title: A scanning tool, not a strategy
items.reveal:
PESTLE (originally PEST, expanded over time) traces to Francis Aguilar's 'Scanning the Business Environment' (1967). It's a structured way to spot environmental change but provides no mechanism to prioritise or combine factors.

Scenario planning (Royal Dutch Shell, from Pierre Wack in the 1970s) goes further: it builds plausible coherent futures and tests strategy against them. PESTLE feeds into scenario planning, not the other way around.
items.why: PESTLE is useful for ensuring you haven't missed an external factor. It's not a strategy tool on its own.

items.title: Maslow's pyramid was never drawn by Maslow
items.claim: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs is taught with a pyramid. What did Maslow himself draw?

options.text: He drew the pyramid himself in his 1943 paper
He never drew it as a pyramid; the pyramid representation was introduced by management consultants and textbooks in the 1960s
He drew it as a circle to indicate non-linear progression
He explicitly rejected any visual representation

items.reveal:
Todd Bridgman, Stephen Cummings and John Ballard's 2019 paper in the Academy of Management Learning & Education traced the pyramid to Charles McDermid's 1960 management article in Business Horizons. Maslow's 1943 'A Theory of Human Motivation' described needs as overlapping and dynamic — not rigidly tiered.

Maslow himself, late in his career, qualified the theory heavily: needs can be pursued in parallel, prioritisation varies by culture and individual, and self-actualisation isn't a 'top' level so much as a developmental orientation.

Empirical tests find weak support for the strict hierarchy.
items.why: The most-taught motivation diagram in business education was drawn by someone other than the named theorist and oversimplifies what he wrote. Worth checking what's in the textbook against what's in the source.
